How to Read a REIT’s Results in 5 Minutes
article:
Singapore real estate investment trusts
(S-REITs) must distribute at least 90% of their taxable income to unitholders to qualify for tax transparency.
This makes them very popular amongst income investors.
But how do you read and analyse a REIT’s financial results?
Results announcements can run to dozens of pages.
Here’s a five-minute checklist covering the five key metrics that matter most.
1. Check Distribution Per Unit
Distribution per unit (DPU) is the most direct measure of the cash income a REIT pays out to its unitholders.
You can compare the latest DPU with the same period a year ago to determine whether it is growing, stable or declining.
A falling or cut DPU is often a
red flag
pointing to rising financing costs, negative rental reversions or loss of major tenants.
It is also important to know if a REIT’s DPU increase comes from recurring income or one-off items.
Parkway Life REIT
(SGX: C2PU), or PLife REIT, for example, paid a DPU of S$0.0877 for 1H2026, up 14.6% from S$0.0765 in 1H2025.
For PLife REIT, gross revenue dipped 1.6% year on year (YoY).
Even so, DPU grew, thanks to higher rental from its Singapore hospitals and nursing homes in France, as well as the absence of a one-off tax provision that had weighed on 1H2025.
In other words, part of the 14.6% jump came from a weaker comparison base, not stronger recurring income.
2. Examine Gross Revenue and Net Property Income (NPI)
Gross revenue refers to the total income generated by a REIT’s properties, while net property income (NPI) is the income remaining after deducting property operating expenses.
Assess whether rental income growth comes from organic growth, such as higher rental rates or acquisitions of additional properties.
This helps determine whether the REIT is improving its existing properties’ performance or simply expanding its portfolio.
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT, reported a 10% YoY increase in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, but the increase came largely from acquisitions such as Paragon, partly offset by properties it sold.
Watch operating expenses too.
If gross revenue grows 5% but NPI grows only 2%, costs are rising faster than rental income.
This is why NPI growth is often a better indicator of underlying property performance, as it reflects the REIT’s ability to generate rental income and manage operating costs effectively.
3. Look at Portfolio Occupancy and Rental Reversion
Portfolio occupancy measures the proportion of a REIT’s total lettable space that is leased.
A high REIT occupancy rate supports stable and recurring rental income.
Declining occupancy may indicate weaker demand or difficulty securing tenants.
Compare the latest occupancy rate with the previous quarter’s to identify whether leasing performance is improving.
CICT, Singapore’s largest REIT, reported committed occupancy of 96.1% for 3Q2026, up from 95.6% in 2Q2026.
The June figure excluded space being renovated at Tampines Mall, while the September figure included it, as that work had been completed.
Investors should also monitor upcoming lease expiries, as major vacancies could affect future rental income.
Rental reversion refers to the change in rental rates when existing leases are renewed or replaced.
Positive rental reversion suggests strong leasing demand and potential rental income growth.
4. Check Gearing and Interest Coverage
A REIT’s gearing ratio measures its borrowings relative to its total assets, indicating how much debt it uses to finance its properties.
Excessive debt increases financial risk, particularly when interest rates rise or property values decline.
Compare the REIT’s aggregate leverage against Singapore’s prevailing regulatory limit of 50%.
Look at the interest coverage ratio (ICR), which measures the REIT’s ability to meet its borrowing costs.
A higher ICR indicates stronger financial flexibility, as the REIT earns several times what it needs to cover its interest bill.
Singapore’s rules require REITs to keep their ICR at a minimum of 1.5 times.
As at 30 June 2026, PLife REIT’s gearing was 33.8% with an ICR of 8.2 times.
CICT’s gearing was 39.7% with an ICR of 3.8 times as at 30 September 2026.
Both are comfortably within the limits, though PLife REIT has more room to absorb higher interest costs.
Investors should also assess how much debt is due for refinancing over the next 12 to 24 months and the proportion of fixed-interest-rate borrowings.
Both show how exposed DPU is to rising interest rates, even when rental income is healthy.
5. Review Net Asset Value and Valuation
Net asset value (NAV) per unit represents the value of a REIT’s total assets after deducting its liabilities, divided by the number of units outstanding.
Changes in property valuations, asset acquisitions and borrowings can all affect NAV per unit.
Investors should compare the REIT’s unit price with its NAV per unit using the price-to-book (P/B) ratio (unit price divided by NAV per unit).
A ratio below 1 indicates that the REIT is trading at a discount to its reported NAV, while a ratio above 1 indicates a premium.
However, trading at a discount does not automatically mean the REIT is undervalued.
It could simply reflect concerns about asset quality, debt levels or future performance.
A REIT’s distribution yield (annual DPU divided by unit price) can reveal whether it’s paying out a generous cash return, but a
high yield
often acts as a warning sign that the market is doubting the safety of those payouts.
Investors should assess whether distributions are sustainable based on earnings and cash flow.
Get Smart: Five Minutes Can Reveal a Lot
Reading REITs’ financial results becomes much easier when you know which numbers to focus on.
DPU reveals the income you receive, revenue and NPI show how the underlying properties are performing, and occupancy and rental reversions offer clues on future rental income.
Gearing and ICR help you assess financial risks, and NAV and valuation aid in deciding if the current unit price is attractive.
Rather than reacting to headlines about a DPU rise or cut, understand what is driving it.
Ultimately, knowing how to read REIT results can help you identify whether a REIT deserves a spot in your portfolio.

title: Yangzijiang Maritime orders 11 newbuilds
article:
Yangzijiang Maritime has ordered 11 additional newbuild vessels, bringing its total newbuilding portfolio to 111 vessels, including options.

The latest orders comprise four bulk carriers of approximately 82,000 DWT (deadweight tonnage) each and seven long-range 2 (LR2) tankers of approximately 114,000 DWT each. The orders are scheduled to be delivered in 2029 and 2030.

The orders for the four bulk carriers also come with options for two additional similar bulk carrier newbuilds.

The latest newbuilds will be funded by a mix of equity co-investment and debt financing.

“Our newbuild strategy is a key differentiator of Yangzijiang Maritime’s business model, enabling us to secure modern vessels at attractive prices and capture value through strategic asset ownership,” says executive chairman and CEO Ren Yuanlin.

“Closely integrated with our proactive asset monetisation strategy, this approach allows us to realise value through vessel sales and redeploy capital into newbuild orders, creating a repeatable cycle of investment and growth within the maritime industry,” he adds.

See also: Keppel extends lease of AD110 rig by five years for US$51 mil

Shares in Yangzijiang Maritime closed 1.5 cents lower or 2.54% down at 57.5 cents on Nov 2.

title: Sats contractors under MOM probe for false occupation and salary declaration of foreign workers
article:
The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) is investigating around 45 companies involved in airport operations at Changi Airport for suspected offences and infringements under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act 1990 (EFMA). The workers are hired by contractors, and sub-contractors of Sats.

At a recent inspection at the airport, MOM found Employment Pass (EP) holders deployed to perform baggage-handling services.

According to MOM's preliminary probes, salaries and occupations declared to MOM for these EP holders were false.

Other work pass holders were also found performing baggage handling work, which was different from their declared occupations.

MOM has so far identified around 270 workers whose deployment may not have been in compliance with work pass regulations.

According to MOM, making a false declaration in a work pass application carries a fine of up to $20,000, imprisonment of up to two years, or both. Employers who illegally deploy a foreign employee may face a financial penalty of up to $10,000. They may also be barred from hiring work pass holders.

See also: LBD Engineering GM charged with operating dormitory without licence, to step down as subsidiary Metrocon's chairman

In its separate statement, Sats says it identified work pass related irregularities involving workers employed by some of its contractors during a routine internal audit.

 

Immediate action was taken against contractor companies who did not meet the standards and obligations required.

"We have since undertaken a broader review of the practices at other contractor companies with whom we work," says Sats, which shared the list of contractor companies and affected workers, identified through its internal audit processes, with MOM.

Since then, SATS has been working closely with MOM and relevant stakeholders in support of their investigations into such practices, and has also enhanced its internal verification process controls.

title: King Wan wins $28.6 mil worth of new M&E contracts
article:
King Wan Corporation announced, on Nov 2, that it has won $28.6 million worth of new mechanical and electrical (M&E) contracts.

The contracts, secured between July and October, are for:
• the design, supply and installation of plumbing, sanitary and gas works, and air-conditioning and mechanical ventilation system works at the 553-unit Lentor Central;
• the design and build of air-conditioning and mechanical ventilation, engineered smoke control and building management system at 51 Tuas View Link; and
• the design, supply, delivery, installation, testing and commissioning of plumbing, sanitary and gas system at the 543-unit River Valley Green.

The projects are slated to be completed between 2028 and 2030.

Shares in King Wan closed 0.1 cent lower or 2.5% down at 3.9 cents on Nov 2.

title: Ray-Ban heir proposes family buyout after €31 bil Czech bid
article:
(Nov 2): Ray-Ban heir Leonardo Maria Del Vecchio proposed buying out his family members from their shared investment vehicle, in a bid to keep the EssilorLuxottica SA eyewear fortune from Czech arms billionare Michal Strnad.

Leonardo Maria outlined his proposal in a letter published in his QN newspaper on Monday. He said he had secured financial backing from an international institution he didn’t identify, and will be ready to present his project to the the seven other shareholders of Delfin Sarl on Nov 7.

“I’ve proposed the total and immediate acquisition of the stakes or other forms of acquisitions more diluted over time,” Leonardo Maria wrote.

The namesake son of EssilorLuxottica founder Leonardo Del Vecchio didn’t disclose any financial details. His project is backed by a €22 billion (US$24.7 billion or $31.6 billion) loan from Citigroup Inc, Corriere della Sera reported. He is offering €3.7 billion each to the other heirs, it said.

Strnad offered on Oct 20 to buy out Delfin at a 30% discount to its net asset value. The offer, made public last week, seeks at least 62.5% of Luxembourg-based Delfin, whose publicly disclosed stakes in listed companies were valued at about €45 billion as of Friday.

See also: Malaysian billionaires said to revive plan to create nation’s biggest mobile operator

A family buyout would accomplish the twin goals of blocking Strnad’s unsolicited approach, while vaulting Leonardo Maria into the dominant position in one of Italy’s most important industrial families. Each of the Del Vecchio heirs owns a 12.5% stake in Delfin, a structure that’s impeded decisionmaking amid infighting by the family members.

The vehicle buying the stakes would have strengthened governance rules and a binding statute, Leonardo Maria wrote. He’ll be flanked by two professionals “with long managerial, legal and financial experience” with binding advice on the most important financial decisions.

Leonardo Maria has made several attempts to buy out his siblings. He proposed €10 billion to buy a combined 25% stake held by Luca and Paola Del Vecchio. The deal hit a wall after lenders lined up to finance it asked for guarantees over Delfin’s investments, which the board denied.

See also: Intel said to buy quantum start-up Classiq for about US$2.3 bil

More recently, his offer to buy out half-brother Rocco Basilico was rejected.

Leonardo Maria, 31, has turned increasingly critical of Francesco Milleri, the chairman of Delfin and chairman and chief executive officer of EssilorLuxottica. He has suggested Milleri was distracted by Delfin’s finanial holdings and blamed him for a drop in EssilorLuxottica shares.

Aside from holding about a third of the eyewear maker, Delfin is also the largest shareholder in Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena SpA, and has played a prominent role in the Italy’s ongoing banking consolidation wave.

title: IndiGo offering lie-flat beds on Airbus A350 to attract long-haul business flyers
article:
(Nov 2): IndiGo will introduce a three-class cabin on its Airbus SE A350 fleet as India’s largest airline broadens its appeal beyond its traditional no-frills offering and expands long-haul operations, its top executive said.

The first A350-900 aircraft are expected to join the fleet in the second quarter of 2028, chief executive officer Willie Walsh told reporters in New Delhi. The configuration for the first 10 aircraft has been finalised and will include 16 lie-flat seats in business class, alongside premium economy and economy cabins.

IndiGo’s push into premium long-haul travel comes as the carrier already dominates India’s domestic aviation market, with a share of around 65%. The A350s will be central to IndiGo’s plan to build a long-haul network, complementing its A321 XLR operations.

The airline had briefly operated long-haul international services using damp-leased Boeing 787-9 aircraft, but has since discontinued those flights.

Walsh said IndiGo, operated by InterGlobe Aviation Ltd, would continue operating A321 XLR services to Amsterdam to retain airport slots until the arrival of the A350 fleet.

Separately, he said the airline was reviewing fuel-hedging policies followed by carriers operating in India. “There are no plans to start hedging until the review is complete,” he said.

See also: JetBlue shares soar after it vows to return to profitability

Walsh also identified Mumbai and the upcoming Navi Mumbai airport as key to IndiGo’s future long-haul growth.

title: Hong Kong chip IPOs tap intertwined networks of investors and bosses
article:
(Nov 2): Hong Kong listing hopefuls are shedding light on the inner workings of their initial public offerings (IPOs), revealing cross-investments and personal connections, just as regulators step up scrutiny of structures that risk distorting the market.

The unusual level of detail was on display last Friday in the prospectus of Hosin Electronics Co, a Chinese memory product maker seeking to raise HK$1.22 billion (US$156 million or $199 million) in an IPO. The company disclosed that a circle of corporate allies and personal acquaintances are among its cornerstone investors — which receive guaranteed allocations in exchange for agreeing to hold the stock for a certain period — who agreed to absorb as much as 42% of the offering.

The Hosin backers include smartphone maker Shenzhen Transsion Holdings Co and chip supplier Shenzhen Longsys Electronics Co. Hosin disclosed that it had also served as a cornerstone backer for both companies’ own Hong Kong listings this year. While Hosin stated that the deals weren’t “inter-conditional”, the dynamic illustrates how industry partners at times become involved in each other’s deals. Hosin’s filing also details how it was introduced to other wealthy investors through acquaintances and industry meet-ups.

The additional disclosures are among the first since Hong Kong regulators started ramping up scrutiny of the city’s booming IPO market to boost transparency and improve the quality of listings. In mid-October, they asked IPO banks to look more closely into potential connections between investors and listing applicants, and to avoid arrangements that could paint an inaccurate picture of buyer demand.

There’s no indication of anything untoward in the type of cross-investment detailed in the Friday filings. Business partners and close allies have long been part of the Hong Kong IPO scene, and there have been similar cases where companies invested in each other’s listings. Hosin and Longsys are strategic partners and both are suppliers to Transsion, their filings showed.

See also: Chinese firm’s investor dispute shows dark side of HK listings

What’s new are the specific disclosures that highlight those relationships more explicitly.

The pattern that emerged in Hosin’s case showed a set of companies that have all invested in each other. Along with Transsion and Longsys, the three companies were cornerstones in each other’s offerings, their filings showed. Transsion has also been active elsewhere, signing up as a pre-IPO shareholder of audio chip company Shanghai FourSemi Semiconductor Co, and backing a fund that was a cornerstone investor in the IPO of diaper brand Softcare Ltd.

Hosin’s offering documents last Friday also lay out how the company became connected with wealthy individual investors in more detail than usual. Former venture capital executive Chen Chun-Cheng and tech industry investor Yeh Pei-Chen both agreed to buy stock after being introduced by an unnamed “mutual acquaintance”, the prospectus showed, without specifying if the same person made both connections.

See also: Chinese PCB maker Dongshan raises US$1.3 bil in HK listing

Liu Ling, a businesswoman who trades electronic components, committed to invest after being introduced by a unspecified member of management, according to the prospectus. Chen Li-Shun, a director at private equity firm MagiCapital, is participating after meeting the company “through an annual investor event”. Another cornerstone investor, W&W Capital Ltd, is part of the same corporate group as an existing Hosin shareholder.

A spokesperson for Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) said the regulator doesn’t comment on individual cases. The spokesperson pointed to an Oct 13 circular, which detailed the responsibility of IPO banks to conduct robust due diligence and “proactively advise” listing applicants on their disclosure obligations.

The SFC urged sponsor banks to “critically assess the commercial substance of transactions, relevant fund flows and investor relationships”. Leaders of the banking syndicates should also inquire about the relationships between a listing applicant and investors, and their implications for the genuineness of investor demand, the SFC said in the October circular.

Other IPOs that launched last Friday also detail existing connections between the companies and their cornerstone investors.

Chinese chip assembly firm Jiangsu Xinde Semiconductor Technology Co lined up three cornerstone buyers that are collectively taking up about a third of its US$130 million offering. The company highlighted that one of them is Suzhou Maxwell Technologies Co, a maker of manufacturing equipment that it said is also one of its suppliers. The prospectus says the cornerstone investment and the companies’ commercial relationship aren’t dependent on each other.

Representatives of Hosin, Longsys and Transsion didn’t immediately respond to requests for comments.

“HKEX is committed to upholding the quality and integrity of Hong Kong’s markets and maintaining high standards of transparency,” the bourse operator said in an emailed statement, declining to comment on specific companies. “Generally speaking, we require the listing applicant to disclose all material information to enable investors to make a properly informed assessment.”

Xinde Semiconductor said in a statement that it maintains an independent supply chain that’s not overly reliant on any single vendor. Some of its packaging lines are compatible with Maxwell equipment, and the two companies’ technical road maps are “broadly aligned”, Xinde Semiconductor said, adding that the cornerstone investment and related commercial arrangements aren’t inter-conditional. Maxwell didn’t immediately respond to queries.
